questions.prompt: For the continuous f graphed below, let g(x)=∫ from 0 to x of f(t) dt. At which interior input does g have a relative maximum?
questions.explanation: FTC gives g′=f. A relative maximum of g requires the derivative to change from positive to negative. The plotted f does that at 5. Its crossing at 1 has the opposite direction; a corner or plateau in f above the axis does not make g turn. A: That sign change is negative to positive and produces a relative minimum of g. B: The integrand f=g′ changes from positive to negative there. C: The positive integrand reaches a plateau there, but g continues increasing. D: The integrand begins decreasing there but remains positive immediately on both sides.

questions.prompt: For f shown in the graph below, define g(x)=∫ from 2 to x of f(t) dt. What is g(0)?
questions.explanation: The graph above the axis on [0,2] is a triangle of base 2 and height 2, with area 2. Since g(0) integrates from 2 back to 0, its signed value is −2. The accumulation is zero at its base input 2, not automatically at input 0. A: This is the integral from 0 to 2 rather than from 2 to 0. B: A zero upper input is not a zero-width integral when the base is 2. C: The positive triangle on [0,2] has area 2, and reversing the bounds negates it. D: This uses a rectangle rather than the triangular area.

questions.prompt: Let g(x)=∫ from 0 to x of the continuous f graphed below. On 0<x<2, which description of g is correct?
options: Increasing and concave up.
Decreasing and concave down.
Increasing and concave down.
Decreasing and concave up.
questions.explanation: The graph of f gives g′, not the height of g. Here f<0, so g decreases. The line rises with slope +1, so g″=f′=1>0 and g is concave up. Its decrease becomes less rapid as the integrand approaches the axis. A: An increasing integrand does not make its accumulation increase when the integrand stays negative. B: The integrand’s positive slope gives positive, not negative, second derivative of g. C: Both the sign and slope translations are reversed. D: The integrand is negative but increasing, so g′<0 and g″>0 there.

questions.prompt: The table below lists a differentiable f and its derivative. If g(x)=∫ from 0 to x of f(t) dt, what is (g′(2),g″(2))?
questions.explanation: FTC yields g′(x)=f(x), and differentiating once more gives g″(x)=f′(x). At input 2 the table shows f(2)=−4 and f′(2)=3, so the pair is (−4,3). Thus g is decreasing and locally concave up at that input. A: FTC gives the ordered pair (f(2),f′(2)). B: This reverses the roles of the first and second accumulation derivatives. C: This takes the second derivative value from the row for input 1. D: The base accumulation g(0)=0 does not make its derivative at 2 zero.

questions.prompt: Suppose f is continuous and strictly positive on [0,4], and g(x)=∫ from 3 to x of f(t) dt. Which description of g at x=2 is justified?
options: Its value is negative, and it is decreasing.
Its value is negative, and it is increasing.
Its value is positive, and it is increasing.
Its value is zero because the integrand is positive.
questions.explanation: Because 2<3, g(2)=−∫ from 2 to 3 of f(t) dt<0. But FTC gives g′(2)=f(2)>0. The accumulated function can be below zero while moving upward; value sign and rate sign measure different features. A: A negative accumulated value does not imply a negative derivative. B: The bounds give a negative accumulated value, while g′(2)=f(2)>0. C: The upper bound 2 lies below the base 3, reversing the positive area. D: Positive integrand gives nonzero area on the nonzero interval from 2 to 3.

questions.prompt: Let g(x)=∫ from 0 to x of (t−1)² dt. What happens to g at x=1?
options: It has a relative maximum.
It has a relative minimum.
It has a horizontal tangent but no relative maximum or minimum.
It is undefined there because the integrand is zero.
questions.explanation: FTC gives g′(x)=(x−1)². This is zero at 1 and positive on each side, so g keeps increasing through the point. Its tangent is horizontal, but there is no local extremum. A zero accumulation derivative alone is not a turning-point test. A: The derivative does not change from positive to negative. B: The derivative does not change from negative to positive. C: The derivative vanishes at 1 yet is positive on both neighboring sides. D: A zero integrand value causes no domain problem for the accumulation.

questions.prompt: For the continuous f in the graph below, define g(x)=∫ from 0 to x of f(t) dt on [0,6]. At which input does g attain its absolute maximum on this closed interval?
questions.explanation: The candidate inputs are endpoints 0 and 6 and the zeros 1 and 5 of f=g′. Geometry gives g(0)=0, g(1)=1, g(5)=−5 and g(6)=−4. The greatest value is 1, attained at input 1. A later rise does not by itself make the final value the largest. A: The initial accumulation is 0, below the positive value at 1. B: That sign crossing produces a local minimum of g. C: The late positive contribution does not recover the earlier accumulated loss. D: The first positive area creates the highest accumulated value before the larger negative contribution.

questions.prompt: Let g(x)=∫ from −2 to x of the continuous f graphed below. Which statement about g at x=0 is correct?
options: It has an inflection point with a nonzero positive slope.
It has a relative minimum because f has a minimum.
It has a horizontal tangent because f changes direction.
It has no derivative because f has a corner.
questions.explanation: FTC gives g′(0)=f(0)=1. To the left, f has slope −1, so g is concave down; to the right, f has slope +1, so g is concave up. The concavity change makes 0 an inflection point of g, despite its nonzero slope and nonexistent second derivative there. A: The integrand changes from decreasing to increasing while its value at 0 stays 1. B: A minimum of the integrand need not be a minimum of the accumulation. C: The slope of g is f(0)=1, not the slope of the integrand. D: Continuity of f suffices for g′ even when f′ fails.

questions.prompt: Use f in the graph below on [2,6]. If g(x)=∫ from 2 to x of f(t) dt, what is g(6)−g(3)?
questions.explanation: Subtracting the two accumulations cancels their common portion from 2 to 3. On [3,4], the remaining positive triangle has area (1/2)·1·3=3/2. On [4,6], the negative triangle contributes −(1/2)·2·6=−6. The difference is 3/2−6=−9/2. A: This reverses the signed accumulation difference. B: The area from 3 to 4 is +3/2 and from 4 to 6 contributes −6. C: This adds the unsigned areas instead of subtracting the negative contribution. D: This includes the extra positive triangle from 2 to 3.

questions.prompt: Let f(x)=(x−2)³+1 and g(x)=∫ from 0 to x of f(t) dt. Which statement about g near x=2 is correct?
options: g has an inflection point because every zero second derivative forces one.
g has a relative maximum because f′(2)=0.
g″(2)=0, but g has no inflection point there.
g has a horizontal tangent at 2.
questions.explanation: FTC gives g′=f and g″=f′=3(x−2)². Although g″(2)=0, it is positive on both sides, so g is concave up through the point rather than changing concavity. Also g′(2)=1, so the tangent is not horizontal. A: A zero second derivative needs an actual concavity change. B: Relative extrema of g depend on the sign change of f, not just a zero of f′. C: The second derivative 3(x−2)² stays positive on both sides. D: The first derivative is f(2)=1.

questions.prompt: Define g(x)=∫ from 0 to x of (2−t) dt for 0≤x≤5. Besides x=0, at which input is g(x)=0?
questions.explanation: The integrand is a line crossing the axis at 2. Its positive triangle on [0,2] has area 2. For x>2 the negative triangular magnitude is (x−2)²/2. Equality with 2 requires x−2=2, giving x=4. This is the nonzero accumulation root in the given domain. A: This is the zero of the integrand and the location of maximum accumulation, not zero accumulation. B: The negative area has not yet cancelled the earlier positive area. C: The negative area already exceeds the earlier positive contribution. D: The negative triangular area from 2 to 4 exactly cancels the positive triangle from 0 to 2.
